clue.text: Day in a western state: or 54 southern ones

definitions.note: The definition is plural and the answer a single continent: the setter names it by counting the countries it is made of, all of them reckoned part of the global south.

indicators.note: Putting one thing in another places it bodily inside, so the letters named first go within the letters named next.

parts.note: the indefinite article taken as the single letter it is
fri is the diary's short form of Friday, one of the days a bare 'day' can stand for
ca is the postal abbreviation for California, on America's west coast

explanation.surface: Weighing up a day spent in one western state against 54 southern ones.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon works as a fence: everything before it builds letters, everything after counts countries. 'State' is an American one in the wordplay and an African one in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The continent is made up of 54 sovereign states, every one of them in the global south, so counting them is a way of naming it.

clue.text: Couple on extreme diet getting increasingly nippy

parts.note: somebody on an extreme diet is fasting, which makes them a faster
a couple is one and another, and the word that couples them sits between the two
the second of the couple, on the same diet and spelt the same way

explanation.surface: A couple on a crash diet feeling the cold more with every day of it.
explanation.walkthrough: Nippy is British for chilly and also for quick; the diet points at the first sense and the grid wants the second. A person who fasts is spelt exactly like the comparative of fast.
explanation.definitionFit: Nippy is everyday British for quick, so something getting increasingly nippy is picking up speed and going on picking it up.

clue.text: Where letters are sorted (to put it briefly)

definitions.meaning: letters of the alphabet are arranged, one after another, inside a word
the phrase that promises to sum something up in the shortest possible space

explanation.surface: A sorting office where the post is put into order.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as the Royal Mail, so 'letters' looks like post and 'sorted' like the job the office does. Both are the alphabet's letters, arranged in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Letters are sorted into their order inside a word, and 'in a word' is also the phrase you use when about to say something in the fewest possible.

clue.text: In regrettable manner, May lashed out

indicators.note: Something out is out of its proper place, and letters out of their proper places have been put in a different order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: A politician called May hitting back at her critics in a way best regretted.
explanation.walkthrough: May comes with a capital and a verb attached, so the eye reads a politician rather than nine loose letters. It is 'out' doing the shuffling, not 'lashed'.
explanation.definitionFit: To do a thing ashamedly is to do it feeling shame over it, which is the manner of someone who regrets what they are doing.

clue.text: Tax idiots, son

parts.note: an ass is a fool, and more than one of them are asses
s is the standard short form for son, as on a family tree

explanation.surface: Telling your son to charge the fools a bit extra.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma turns 'son' into somebody being spoken to, which is where the clue parks its final letter. 'Tax' is the verb here rather than the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To assess is to fix the sum someone owes, which is what 'tax' means as a verb — the taxman assesses you and taxes you in the same breath.

clue.text: Pretended to have served well with time invested

indicators.note: Money invested is money put into something, and a letter invested goes inside the word already built.

parts.note: to ace a serve is to send down one the other player never touches
t is the standard short form for time

explanation.surface: Somebody claiming a fine record of service now the years have been put in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Served well' sounds like a career in the forces or behind a bar; on a tennis court it is the serve nobody returns. What is invested here is a letter, not money.
explanation.definitionFit: To act is to put on a show of feeling something you do not feel, so 'acted' and 'pretended' are the same past tense.

clue.text: Nightcap perhaps when retiring — retired with some Bass?

indicators.note: To retire is to withdraw, to go back the way you came, so the letters assembled are read back to front.

parts.note: ret. is the standard short form of retired, as it follows an officer's name
a bass is a fish, and some of what a fish is equipped with are its fins

explanation.surface: A drink before bed with a retired friend and a few bottles of Bass.
explanation.walkthrough: Bass the beer pours the drink on the surface and bass the fish supplies the letters. 'Retiring' and 'retired' stand side by side doing different jobs, one turning the letters round, the other an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A snifter is a small drink taken for pleasure, and the one taken last thing before bed is a nightcap — one instance of the class, as 'perhaps' warns.

clue.text: Cover wounds with this lipstick — strange, strange

indicators.note: The word comes round a second time, and the second one is the instruction: what is strange is not as it was, so the letters before it settle in another order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, fifteen letters

explanation.surface: Using some peculiar lipstick to cover up wounds.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeat is the whole trick: the first 'strange' is material and the second is the instruction. A sticking plaster is what Britain calls the little adhesive dressing sold elsewhere as a Band-Aid.
explanation.definitionFit: A sticking plaster is the small adhesive dressing you press over a cut, so covering wounds is the entire job it exists for.

clue.text: Heap sitting coiled?

indicators.note: Something coiled has been wound out of its straight line, and letters wound out of line no longer read in the order given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

explanation.surface: A pile of something sitting wound round on itself.
explanation.walkthrough: Read straight the clue describes the thing; read as an instruction its first two words are the letters. Spaghettini is spaghetti's thinner cousin, and the question mark admits the description would fit other pasta too.
explanation.definitionFit: Spaghettini is a fine spaghetti, and a serving of it does sit on the plate as a coiled heap — the clue read straight.

clue.text: Primarily, cannelloni; alternatively, rye bread?

indicators.note: What comes primarily comes first, so each word after it gives up its opening letter and nothing more.

parts.note: the opening letter of each of the four words in turn

explanation.surface: Working out supper: pasta for preference, or failing that some rye bread.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word pulls double duty — read straight they are examples of the thing, read down their initials they spell it. Even 'alternatively', which looks like pure joinery, is holding a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Carb is the everyday shortening of carbohydrate, and pasta and bread are the two staples anybody using the word has in mind.

clue.text: Went on horseback where you may travel loudly

indicators.note: Said loudly means said out loud, so what is wanted is the word that sounds like the description rather than the one spelt that way.

parts.note: a road is where you may travel, and the past tense of ride says the same thing aloud

explanation.surface: Somebody making a thoroughly noisy journey along the highway.
explanation.walkthrough: Both spellings run to four letters and both open with the same sound, so 'loudly' is the only thing telling you which one the grid wants.
explanation.definitionFit: To ride is to travel on a horse, and the past tense is what 'went on horseback' asks for.

clue.text: Was that infuriating? Don't be ridiculous

definitions.note: The clue's first half asks about the event and the answer asks the person, but the enquiry is the same one: whether anger has been caused.
definitions.meaning: the question you put to someone who has just been provoked, mad meaning angry
the retort flung at a daft suggestion, mad meaning out of your senses

explanation.surface: One person checking whether something annoyed you and then telling you not to be silly.
explanation.walkthrough: Mad covers anger at one end and lunacy at the other, and the clue takes one sense in each half. Neither question expects an answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Asking whether someone is mad can mean asking whether they are angry, and thrown at a daft plan the same words mean exactly 'don't be ridiculous'.

clue.text: In the direction of Kentucky, reaching old capital

indicators.note: To reach something is to extend as far as it, so what has been built runs straight on into the letter named next.

parts.note: heading in the direction of a place is going to it
ky is the two-letter postal abbreviation for the state of Kentucky
o is the standard short form for old

explanation.surface: Travelling towards Kentucky and arriving at some ancient capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old capital' invites a city that has lost the job to Kyoto or Edo; 'old' is only a letter, and the capital in the answer still holds the post.
explanation.definitionFit: Tokyo is the capital of Japan, so 'capital' names it as one city of that kind.

clue.text: In bed, Sally's twisted

indicators.note: Something in a thing sits inside it, so the word named straight after closes round what comes next.

parts.note: the bed the surface puts her in, taken as its own three letters
a sally is a sudden dash out at the enemy, which is a raid

explanation.surface: Sally lying in bed in a tangle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twisted' looks like an instruction to shuffle and is the definition instead — this clue is built, not stirred. A sally is the rush out from a besieged position.
explanation.definitionFit: Braided hair or rope has been twisted strand over strand, so 'twisted' describes exactly what has been done to it.

clue.text: Ernest rang Ethel — a little odd

indicators.note: A little of something is a part of it and not the whole, so only a short run of the letters on offer is wanted.

parts.note: the run starts two letters into the first name and stops at the start of the third

explanation.surface: Ernest making a slightly peculiar telephone call to Ethel.
explanation.walkthrough: Three names in a row read as the cast of a little story rather than as material. 'A little odd' looks like one phrase and is really instruction plus definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Odd and strange both mean out of the ordinary, and either adjective drops into the same slot in a sentence.

clue.text: Collective musical activity getting ganglions tingling

indicators.note: A thing tingling will not keep still, and letters that will not keep still end up in another arrangement.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Group music-making that sets the nerve clusters buzzing.
explanation.walkthrough: Ganglions are clusters of nerve cells, so the tingling on the surface is medical rather than musical. Nine letters of anatomy, nine letters of answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A singalong is an occasion where everyone present sings the same songs together, which is music made collectively rather than performed at anybody.

clue.text: Propriety, almost ideal!? Complete mess!

indicators.note: Almost a word is the word one letter short of finished, so the last letter never arrives.
To complete a thing is to finish it off, so what is named next goes on the end of what has been built.

parts.note: an ideal is a model, and the last letter of MODEL is dropped
a sty is the byword for a filthy mess of a room

explanation.surface: Something that started out nearly perfect and ended up a total shambles.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics mark 'almost' as an instruction rather than part of the exclamation. A sty is the pig's pen, and any room left in that state gets called one.
explanation.definitionFit: Modesty is keeping a proper restraint about yourself, which is propriety in the matter of how you behave and what you claim.

clue.text: Bare Everyman: concerning!

parts.note: Everyman sets this puzzle, so the name in the clue is the setter calling himself me
re is the everyday shorthand for concerning, as at the head of a memo

explanation.surface: The setter turning up with no clothes on, which is a worry.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman signs himself into his own clues, so wherever the name appears it is the setter speaking of himself. 'Concerning' is the memo-heading preposition, not the adjective the exclamation mark suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: A mere formality is a bare formality — both words cut the thing down to nothing more than the name it is given.

clue.text: They carry swords in aquariums — no question that's dodgy

indicators.note: Saying there is none of a thing takes it away, so the letters it stands for come out before anything else happens.
Something dodgy cannot be trusted to be what it looks like, and letters that cannot be trusted shift into another order.

parts.note: the letters to work with, before two of them go
qu. is the standard short form of question, and those are the two letters taken out

explanation.surface: Fish that carry swords kept in tanks, and something shady about the whole business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They carry swords in aquariums' paints swordfish, which is why the tanks read as scenery rather than as material. The letters that leave are spelt out by 'question', not merely implied.
explanation.definitionFit: The samurai were the sword-bearing warrior class of feudal Japan, known above all for the pair of blades worn at the waist.

clue.text: 'Hardly commercial', describing episode in paper

indicators.note: To describe a circle is to draw right round it, so the words before this one wrap themselves about what comes next.

parts.note: a commercial is an ad, so something hardly commercial is not ad
ep is the standard short form for an episode of a series

explanation.surface: A review calling one episode of something anything but commercial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In paper' reads as where the review appeared; 'paper' is the definition and 'in' only joins it on. The quotation marks flag the opening phrase as words to be taken at face value.
explanation.definitionFit: A notepad is a block of paper for jotting on, so the bare word 'paper' covers it the way it covers anything you write on.

clue.text: Remove parody

definitions.meaning: what you do to a coat, a lid, or ten per cent of the bill
an impersonation that exaggerates whoever it copies

explanation.surface: A curt order to get rid of a spoof.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words, two definitions, and the hyphen in the enumeration is the hint that they belong to one phrase. The verb loses its space to become the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To take a thing off is to remove it, and a take-off of somebody is a mocking impersonation of them.

clue.text: Crossword setter ran flipping fancy food emporium

indicators.note: To flip a thing is to turn it over, so the letters built up so far are read from the far end back.

parts.note: the setter writing the clue speaks of himself as I
to run a company or a meeting is to lead it

explanation.surface: A crossword setter who used to run some blessed posh food shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' is mild British swearing on the surface and the turn in the wordplay. 'Ran' is past tense, so the word standing in for it has to be past tense too.
explanation.definitionFit: A deli sells cured meats, cheeses and olives rather than ordinary groceries, which puts it at the fancy end of the food shop.

clue.text: Once more, fortify bottom before getting married

indicators.note: One thing before another stands in front of it, so the letters named first take the front of the answer.

parts.note: the rear is the back of anything, and politely a person's bottom
m is the standard short form for married, as on a form

explanation.surface: One last session firming up your backside before the wedding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fortify' reads as toning muscle and means supplying weapons. The comma after 'more' is the seam: the definition is two words that would ordinarily sit the other way round.
explanation.definitionFit: To rearm is to take up weapons again, so fortifying once more is exactly the job the word does.

clue.text: Ban #8

parts.note: the eight on an American pool table is the black one
and the hash sign numbers a ball, which is the thing the eight is

explanation.surface: A curt instruction to bar number eight.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words of clue and no wordplay words at all: '#8' is the black ball of American pool, written the way a shirt number is. Clubs once voted on members by dropping balls in a box, a black one meaning no.
explanation.definitionFit: To blackball someone is to vote against letting them into a club, which bans them from joining it.

clue.text: Display of delight about river fish

indicators.note: To be about something is to be all round it, so the word named first closes over the letter that follows.

parts.note: a beam is the wide smile delight puts on a face
r is the standard short form for river, as on a map

explanation.surface: Delight at the news about the fish in the river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like the preposition that introduces a topic and is the instruction to go round instead. The definition is the last word on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A bream is a broad, deep-bodied freshwater fish of the carp family, so 'fish' names the kind of thing it is.

clue.text: Twitching poet to board warship

indicators.note: Something twitching is jerking about without control, and letters jerked about do not stay in the order they were given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

explanation.surface: A jittery poet being taken aboard a warship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To board' looks like the poet's errand and is part of the material, which leaves the final word alone to do the defining.
explanation.definitionFit: A torpedo boat is a small fast naval craft built round its torpedo tubes, so it is a warship of one particular kind.

clue.text: Trump, snubbed, is to be arrested: that's stating the obvious

definitions.note: The clue's phrase names the act of saying it while the answer names the remark itself, which is how such a remark is always labelled.

indicators.note: To snub someone is to cut them short, and a word cut short loses the letter on its end.
Being arrested is being seized and held, so the letters named are held inside the ones around them.

parts.note: the name with its final letter cut away
the word itself, dropped into the gap

explanation.surface: Donald Trump being cut dead and then taken into custody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' looks like the sentence's verb and is two of the answer's letters. The colon marks where the building stops and the defining starts.
explanation.definitionFit: A truism is a remark so obviously true that saying it tells nobody anything, which is what stating the obvious produces.

clue.text: Wanting some, dreaming of erstwhile errand-boys?

indicators.note: Wanting some of a thing asks for a part of it rather than the whole, so a run of letters is taken from inside what follows.

parts.note: the run starts on the last letter of the first word and stops three letters into the last

explanation.surface: Somebody hankering after the days when you could send a lad out on errands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Erstwhile' is the scenery that makes the run look like nostalgia, and it is carrying three letters while it does it. A gofer is the junior sent to go for the coffee and the post.
explanation.definitionFit: A gofer is the dogsbody sent to fetch whatever is wanted, which is the errand-boy's job under a newer name.
